summary.text: For every \(1\le d\le2025\), a finite check among the primes \(\{2,3,5,7,11,13,19\}\) finds \(p,q\) with different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither dividing \(d\). Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some \(i<pq\le150\) has \(pq\mid a+id\), forcing that term to have prime divisors with two different final digits.

full_proof.text:
We prove the stronger statement that no such arithmetic progression exists.

Call a positive integer \(n>1\) lopsided if the set
\[
 R(n)=\{p\bmod 10:p\text{ is a prime divisor of }n\}
\]
has at most one element. Thus, to prove that a number is not lopsided, it suffices to find two prime divisors of it having different final decimal digits.

Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) such that
\[
 a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025,
\]
and all 150 integers
\[
 a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

We first establish a finite lemma about the possible prime divisors of \(d\).

Consider the following pairs of primes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13),(2,19),\\
 &(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,19),\\
 &(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),(5,19),\\
 &(7,11),(7,13),(7,19),\\
 &(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
In every listed pair \((p,q)\), the two entries are prime, they have different final decimal digits, and their product is at most 150. For completeness, their products, in the order displayed, are
\[
 6,10,14,22,26,38,
 15,21,33,57,
 35,55,65,95,
 77,91,133,
 143,
\]
all at most 150. The final digits involved are respectively those of the primes
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,19,
\]
namely \(2,3,5,7,1,3,9\), and direct comparison confirms that the two digits differ for every pair in (1).

We claim that, because \(d\le 2025\), at least one pair \((p,q)\) in (1) has the property that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\).

Assume otherwise. Then every pair in (1) has at least one member dividing \(d\). In graph terminology, the primes dividing \(d\) form a vertex cover of the graph whose edges are the pairs (1), but we give the complete elementary case analysis.

Among the five primes
\[
 2,3,5,7,11,
\]
every pair occurs in (1): the ten relevant pairs are
\[
\begin{gathered}
(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),\quad
(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),\\
(5,7),(5,11),\quad (7,11).
\end{gathered}
\]
Consequently, at most one of \(2,3,5,7,11\) can fail to divide \(d\). Indeed, if two of them failed to divide \(d\), the pair formed by those two primes would be a pair in (1) neither of whose members divides \(d\), contrary to our present assumption.

We now exhaust the six possibilities.

1. If none of \(2,3,5,7,11\) is omitted, then all five divide \(d\). Since these are distinct primes, their product divides \(d\), so
\[
 d\ge 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>2025.
\]

2. Suppose \(2\nmid d\). Then \(3,5,7,11\) all divide \(d\). Moreover, the pairs \((2,13)\) and \((2,19)\) occur in (1). Since \(2\) does not divide \(d\), our assumption that each listed pair has a member dividing \(d\) forces both \(13\mid d\) and \(19\mid d\). Hence
\[
 3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot19=285285
\]
divides \(d\), which is impossible when \(d\le2025\).

3. Suppose \(3\nmid d\). Then \(2,5,7,11\) all divide \(d\). The pair \((3,19)\) forces \(19\mid d\). Therefore
\[
 2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot19=14630
\]
divides \(d\), again contradicting \(d\le2025\).

4. Suppose \(5\nmid d\). Then \(2,3,7,11\) divide \(d\). The pairs \((5,13)\) and \((5,19)\) force \(13\mid d\) and \(19\mid d\). Thus
\[
 2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot19=114114
\]
divides \(d\), impossible for \(d\le2025\).

5. Suppose \(7\nmid d\). Then \(2,3,5,11\) divide \(d\). The pairs \((7,13)\) and \((7,19)\) force \(13\mid d\) and \(19\mid d\). Thus
\[
 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13\cdot19=81510
\]
divides \(d\), again impossible.

6. Finally, suppose \(11\nmid d\). Then \(2,3,5,7\) divide \(d\). The pair \((11,13)\) forces \(13\mid d\). It follows that
\[
 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730
\]
divides \(d\), which is still greater than 2025.

In each case, the assertion that the displayed product divides \(d\) follows because all its factors are distinct primes and hence pairwise coprime. Since \(d\ge1\), divisibility by a positive integer \(M\) implies \(d\ge M\). Every case therefore contradicts \(d\le2025\).

This proves the finite lemma: there is a pair \((p,q)\) in (1) such that
\[
 p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d.
\tag{2}
\]
Fix such a pair. By construction, \(p\) and \(q\) are primes, their last decimal digits differ, and
\[
 pq\le150.
\tag{3}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(d\), we have \(\gcd(d,p)=1\). Similarly, \(\gcd(d,q)=1\). Also \(p\ne q\), since their last digits differ. It follows that
\[
 \gcd(d,pq)=1.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\).

We next use (4) to find one of the first 150 terms divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\). The congruence
\[
 a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}
\tag{5}
\]
has a solution because \(d\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(pq\): explicitly, if \(d^{-1}\) denotes such an inverse, take
\[
 i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq}.
\]
Choose the least nonnegative representative of this residue class. Then
\[
 0\le i<pq.
\]
Together with (3), this gives
\[
 0\le i<150.
\tag{6}
\]
Equation (5) says exactly that
\[
 pq\mid a+id.
\]
Therefore both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\).

The integer \(a+id\) is positive—and in fact at least \(a\ge2\)—because \(i\ge0\) and \(d\ge1\). Hence \(p\) and \(q\) are genuine prime divisors of this term. Their final decimal digits are different, so the set of final digits of the prime divisors of \(a+id\) contains at least the two distinct elements
\[
 p\bmod10\quad\text{and}\quad q\bmod10.
\]
Thus \(a+id\) is not lopsided.

But (6) shows that \(a+id\) is one of the assumed 150 terms, contradicting the assumption that all of them are lopsided. Therefore there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which every term \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), belongs to A381159. This disproves the conjectured positive answer.
